label: AQ 0022
title: The agents that stopped adding up

questions.q: MacNet says many systems run below their potential and should add agents. Doesn't that back leadership?
questions.a: Only partly. MacNet (Qian et al., ICLR 2025) measured GPT-3.5 on four benchmarks, and 64 nodes was the end of its range. Its hundred-agent saturation counts agents on the links too, so a sparse shape gets there between 32 and 64 nodes; it called 16 nodes a reasonable choice, balancing quality against cost. Test on our own tasks before believing the next two steps.

teach.title: How it works: the shape, the cost and the stopping rule

questions.q: Does it matter if all 64 agents run the same model?
questions.a: Yes. My reasoning: copies of one model tend to make the same mistakes. In Mixture-of-Agents (Wang et al., 2024), six different models as proposers reached a 61.3% win rate on AlpacaEval 2.0 (a judge compares each answer with a reference model's, adjusted for length), against 56.7% for six answers sampled from one model. Variety can buy more than headcount.

teach.title: How it works: the shape, the cost and the stopping rule

questions.q: How would you find the knee without running 64 agents on everything?
questions.a: Run 16, 32 and 64 on a few hundred tasks and split the results by difficulty. Chen et al. showed voting can help easy questions and hurt hard ones, so the overall curve can peak and fall; they estimate the best number of calls from a small sample.

teach.title: How it works: the shape, the cost and the stopping rule

questions.q: What shape did the MacNet study find as networks of agents grew?
questions.a: An S-shaped (logistic) curve against network size on a doubling scale: slow, then steep, then flat. Most of its topologies saturated at about a hundred agents, counting agents on the links too: between 32 and 64 nodes in a chain, star or tree.

teach.title: How it works: the shape, the cost and the stopping rule

questions.q: In Kim et al.'s Google study, how did coordination turns grow with the number of agents?
questions.a: Faster than the agent count: their fitted curve is turns ≈ 2.72 × (n + 0.5) to the power 1.724. Extrapolated, it gives about 69 turns at six agents, against 7.2 for a single agent, all from the same token budget.

teach.title: How it works: the shape, the cost and the stopping rule

questions.q: 16 agents cost $0.80 a task and solve 72%; 64 agents cost $3.20 and solve 76%. What does each extra solved task cost?
questions.a: $60: the extra $2.40 per task, spread over 0.04 extra solves per task (2.40 ÷ 0.04).
